 Pinned Updated   Nov. 3, 2026, 8:17 p.m. ET Kellen Browning 
 Here’s the latest. 
 Senator Jon Ossoff of Georgia, a Democrat, fended off his challenger in a crucial battleground race, according to The Associated Press, dealing a blow to Republicans’ hopes of flipping a seat in the fight for control of Congress. Polls had shown the Georgia race slipping away from Representative Mike Collins, a Republican, in a tough national environment for the party.
 Polls have also closed in battleground states including Ohio, South Carolina, Florida and Maine, which all feature competitive races. Turnout appeared strong across the country , as millions of people cast votes that will deliver a verdict on an unpopular president who has implored the country to act as if he were on the ballot.
 Democratic candidates have blamed President Trump, and the war he started this year in Iran, for the economic hardships that have driven a current of frustration across the nation. Republicans have focused on portraying their Democratic opponents as extreme on social issues and the economy as they played defense in reliably red states.
 Favorable polling has buoyed Democrats’ hopes of taking control of the House, but Republicans have worked to protect their majority with aggressive redistricting efforts. In the Senate, Republicans sought to use their fund-raising advantage to protect seats in traditionally conservative strongholds, including Texas and Kansas, where some polling places have closed.
 In Florida, Democrats turned back an attempt by Republicans to flip two seats via redistricting: Representative Jared Moskowitz and Representative Kathy Castor won re-election in districts that Republicans redrew in an effort to oust them. Early returns showed tight races for embattled Republican incumbents in the House, including Anna Paulina Luna, a star among the MAGA faithful. Later-reporting returns from Election Day were expected to favor Republicans.
 In South Carolina, Senator Darline Graham has been filling the seat long occupied by her late brother, Lindsey, and Democrats have hoped that Dr. Annie Andrews, a pediatrician, could flip the seat. In Ohio — which also features an acrimonious race for governor — former Senator Sherrod Brown, a Democrat, is vying for a comeback as he tries to oust Senator Jon Husted, a Republican. In North Carolina, former Gov. Roy Cooper faces Michael Whatley, the former chairman of the Republican National Committee, as he tries to flip a seat to Democrats.
 In Virginia, both parties were monitoring two races — the First District, which Democrats were hoping they could flip, and another competitive contest in the Fifth District.
 The last polling places will not close until 1 a.m. Eastern on Wednesday, in Alaska. Full results won’t be known until well into the evening — and maybe not for days or longer , particularly if many of the races are close — but it’s clear that voters were eager to have their say. In each of the major Senate battlegrounds, including Texas, North Carolina and Michigan, early turnout eclipsed that of the last midterm cycle.
 In Texas, overall turnout could exceed 10 million votes, which would top the total from each of the last two midterms. In Georgia, Election Day turnout was on track to beat that of the 2024 presidential election, the Georgia secretary of state said.
 Here’s what else we’re covering:
 A complicated landscape: More than 400 Times reporters, editors, data analysts, video journalists and photographers are covering the midterms, seeking to understand a large country with voters who are complicated — and sometimes contradictory. Read more › 
 The counting process: Control of the Senate will hinge on the outcomes in the battleground states of Alaska, Iowa, Kansas, Maine, Michigan, Minnesota, Nebraska, New Hampshire, Ohio, South Carolina and Texas. Here’s when to expect results › 
 Big spending: This is the most expensive midterm election, as measured in spending on political advertising, since at least 2018, according to data from AdImpact. Elon Musk, the world’s richest person, alone contributed $474 million to Republican groups, candidates and their allies, more than any donor has ever spent in a single election cycle. Read more › 
 Minor disruptions: A technical problem with voting machines in Westchester County, N.Y., outside New York City , led officials there to collect ballots by hand in a competitive House race. In Florida, flooding forced more than 20 polling stations across eight counties to be relocated. In North Carolina, technical problems at several precincts caused minor delays; state election officials said they would delay the release of election results to at least 8:15 p.m. from 7:30 p.m. Read more › 
 Election integrity: Many election officials and Democrats have said they fear that Mr. Trump’s attacks on the integrity of U.S. elections could lead to tensions during voting and baseless challenges to the outcome. The administration has sought to prove that many noncitizens have cast ballots, but few people have been charged with offenses related to voting fraud. Local and state officials say they are well prepared to run a secure election .
 Court rulings: A federal judge has turned down a request by Democratic lawmakers and party organizations to prohibit the Trump administration from coercing states into screening incoming ballots. And the Supreme Court issued what appeared to be an extraordinary rebuke to Mr. Trump, signaling that it was not interested in assisting his efforts to interfere with how states administer elections.

 Democrats hold on to a critical Senate seat in New Hampshire. 
 Image Chris Pappas has served for four terms in the House. Credit... John Tully for The New York Times Representative Chris Pappas, a Democrat, has won the Senate race in New Hampshire, according to The Associated Press , holding a seat for his party in a purple state that both parties viewed as critical. His victory makes him the first openly gay man in U.S. history to win a Senate seat.
 Mr. Pappas defeated John E. Sununu, a former senator who lost re-election in 2008. A scion of a Republican political family whose father and brother served as governor, Mr. Sununu sought to present himself as distinct from President Trump’s MAGA movement. But he was unable to overcome the distaste for the president in New Hampshire, which has never backed Mr. Trump in a presidential election.
 Mr. Pappas, 46, has represented the state’s swingy First Congressional District for four terms with an understated political style mirroring that of Senator Jeanne Shaheen, the retiring Democrat he is set to replace. (Ms. Shaheen beat Mr. Sununu in 2008.)
 During his campaign, Mr. Pappas spoke little of the history he would make if he won, saying in interviews that he preferred to keep the focus on voters, not on himself. But gay rights advocates around the nation celebrated his victory as a sign of progress nearly four decades after Barney Frank of Massachusetts became the first gay member of Congress to come out voluntarily, in 1987.
 “The fact is, I’m living a reality today that I didn’t think was possible when I was growing up just a few decades ago,” Mr. Pappas said in an interview during the campaign. “My state, our country, has come a long way.”
 A son of Manchester, N.H., who came home after college to work at his family’s restaurant and run for local office, Mr. Pappas sought to nationalize the race, repeatedly reminding voters that Senate control could run through the state.
 He called Mr. Sununu “another vote for Donald Trump’s failed, reckless agenda” and framed his opponent as a pillar of the status quo. He ignored the fact that it was he, not Mr. Sununu, who had spent much of the past 20 years in elected office.
 The Sununu name is so prominent in the state that Mr. Pappas and his allies frequently joked that voters did not actually know which member of the family was on the ballot. Mr. Sununu’s charismatic brother, Chris, served as governor from 2017 to 2025; his father, John H. Sununu, was George H.W. Bush’s chief of staff and the New Hampshire governor from 1983 to 1989.
 John E. Sununu, 62, worked aggressively to distance himself from Mr. Trump on issues like tariffs and the war with Iran, hoping to appeal to independent voters and moderate Republicans. He ran an ad saying he had “never even met the man.” And he framed his candidacy as being about what comes after Mr. Trump.
 “In two years, the president will leave office,” Mr. Sununu said during a debate last month. “And my question is, where do we go next?”
 The answer New Hampshire voters delivered was: Not back to a candidate many associated with the past.

 Data reporter In the Florida Senate race, the state’s three Hispanic-majority counties are all shifting drastically to the left, providing some early insights into a demographic that will be closely watched nationwide.
 President Trump swept Miami-Dade, Hendry and Osceola counties in 2024. But this year, each swung toward Angie Nixon, the Democratic nominee, by at least 18 percentage points. That was enough to flip both Miami-Dade and Osceola, while Ashley Moody, the Republican nominee, held on to Hendry County despite a nearly 27-point swing to the left.

 Congressional reporter Georgia was always expected to be a state where a significant number of voters might split their tickets between the Senate and governor’s races, and the results so far suggest that expectation is holding true. Senator Jon Ossoff, a Democrat, has won re-election, defeating his Republican challenger, Representative Mike Collins, while former Mayor Keisha Lance Bottoms of Atlanta, a Democrat, holds a narrower lead over Rick Jackson, a Republican, in the governor’s race. The disparity suggests that some voters who backed Ossoff were less willing to support his fellow Democrat for governor. Musk spent over $200 million to try to elect Ken Paxton, a Republican, to the Senate in his home state.  Congressional reporter Juliana Stratton, the Democratic lieutenant governor of Illinois, defeated Don Tracy, a former state Republican Party chairman, in the state’s Senate race, according to The Associated Press. Stratton’s victory means that next year, three Black women will serve in the Senate at the same time — a first in the institution’s history.
 When she takes office, she will serve alongside Senator Tammy Duckworth, a Thai American, making Illinois the first state represented by two women of color in the Senate at the same time.

 Video What to Watch in Texas Could Texas elect its first Democratic Senator in decades? Our election data reporter Christine Zhang tells us what counties to watch in the competitive Texas Senate race. Nov. 3, 2026, 8:03 p.m. ET Christine Zhang 
 Election data reporter Kansas, where polls closed at 8 p.m. Eastern, has been reliably red in federal races, but the state has moved leftward in recent years and has had a Democratic governor since 2019. The Senate race between Roger Marshall, the Republican incumbent, and Adam Hamilton, his Democratic challenger, will hinge on counties Democrats have carried in presidential races, as well as areas that supported the re-election of Gov. Laura Kelly, a Democrat, in 2022 and voted for President Trump two years later.
 Johnson County , a suburb of Kansas City where Hamilton lives, will account for over a quarter of the vote. Democrats won Johnson by over eight percentage points in the 2020 and 2024 presidential elections, but Hamilton is looking to make even more inroads there. In the 2022 governor’s race, Kelly won it by 20 points. Sedgwick County , which contains Wichita, is a key bellwether and a target for both candidates: Kelly won the county by three points, while Trump won it by more than 13 in 2024. Shawnee County , which contains Topeka, could provide an early read on the race; in 2024 it had mostly finished reporting its votes by 10 p.m. Eastern. Like Sedgwick, it was much bluer in the governor’s race: Kelly carried it by about 20 points, while Kamala Harris won it by less than one.

 Reporting from South Carolina Jon Ossoff rides viral videos to easy win in Georgia Senate race. 
 Image Jon Ossoff, who has served one term in the Senate, was an exceptional campaign fund-raiser. Credit... Alex Kent/The New York Times Senator Jon Ossoff of Georgia, whose race was a must-win for Democrats, easily won re-election on Tuesday, according to The Associated Press . His commanding victory is sure to catapult his name into more conversations about potential 2028 presidential contenders .
 Mr. Ossoff, a first-term incumbent, defeated Representative Mike Collins, the Republican nominee, who faced accusations of bigotry and trailed throughout the campaign.
 Mr. Ossoff’s feat was by no means a given. He entered the midterms as the only Democrat trying to hold on to a Senate seat in a state that President Trump won in 2024. That made Mr. Ossoff, at least on paper, the most vulnerable Senate Democrat seeking re-election this year. Democrats needed to hold on to the seat to have any realistic chance of winning Senate control.
 But Mr. Ossoff proved an exceptional fund-raiser and an aggressive anti-Trump campaigner, giving fiery speeches that yielded viral video clips in which he accused the president and his family of corruption and the Trump administration of threatening American democracy. He denounced Mr. Trump and his allies as the “Epstein class” and the “Mar-a-Lago mafia”; both phrases were a hit with Democrats and gave Mr. Ossoff the air of a liberal populist.
 His ability to tie corruption to the high cost of living, weaving a broader criticism of money in politics rigging the system against regular voters, fueled speculation about possible White House ambitions. Mr. Ossoff, 39, has disavowed any interest in seeking the presidency and has said that he will serve a full six-year Senate term.
 Mr. Collins, a two-term congressman from Jackson, Ga., won the Republican primary by campaigning as a Trump loyalist, defeating a more moderate candidate backed by Gov. Brian Kemp, who polling suggests is the state’s most popular Republican by far. Mr. Kemp would have quite likely given Mr. Ossoff a tougher challenge, but he passed on a Senate run, leaving some Georgia Republicans anxious that they might be poorly positioned to defeat Mr. Ossoff in a tough year for their party.
 From the start, Mr. Ossoff went after Mr. Collins, 59, hard. He attacked him for reposting a video in 2024 of white male students taunting and jeering at a female Black student with racist and profane remarks — and for his history of having aides who espoused white nationalist and antisemitic views. Mr. Collins said in a debate last month that he had “condemned racism, antisemitism, hate.”
 But Mr. Collins struggled to make a case that Mr. Ossoff was elitist and out of touch, or that his own experience as the owner of a trucking company made him better suited to represent regular Georgians.
 By the fall, Mr. Collins’s polling numbers looked so dismal that Republicans began to shift resources away from the race, making Georgia the first big state to all but fall off the competitive Senate map.

 More federal election monitors than ever have been fanned out to polling places. 
 Image Voters at Henry Ford High School in Detroit, where federal monitors were stationed on Tuesday. Credit... Victor J. Blue for The New York Times For decades, the Justice Department has sent monitors to observe polling places on Election Day and ensure that local officials are complying with federal civil rights laws.
 But the Trump administration’s decision to significantly expand the program and send roughly 1,000 monitors to all 50 states on Tuesday caused Democrats and voting-rights advocates nationwide to fear that federal officials would interfere with voters casting ballots. President Trump has repeatedly made false claims about widespread election fraud , mobilized law enforcement officials to investigate voters and asked judges to intervene in state-administered elections. The Justice Department said that it had conducted its largest monitoring effort ever this year.
 On Tuesday, local and state officials nationwide said the monitors had largely behaved in keeping with past elections and had not tried to interfere with or intimidate voters, although there were reports of what appeared to be minor friction.
 In heavily Democratic Bernalillo County, N.M., Justice Department monitors asked voters “unusual questions,” according to a spokeswoman for the secretary of state’s office. State election officials complained to the Justice Department but had received “no additional reports of similar behavior” since, the spokeswoman said.
 In Michigan, state officials said they reached out to the Justice Department after receiving reports of improprieties in Dearborn, Flint and Lansing. Among them: federal monitors asking poll workers for their training materials and trying to speak with voters inside polling places — both of which violated their agreements with local officials. No further problems had been reported as of late Tuesday afternoon, state officials said.
 Even before Election Day, local governments from Arkansas to Minnesota had decided to bar federal monitors from entering polling places, requiring them to observe from outside instead. In New Haven, Conn., local election officials told the Justice Department in a letter that “rhetoric and federal actions” appeared to be intended to “cast doubt on election integrity and to intimidate voters,” and wrote that they would deny access to the monitors.
 In a social media post, the Justice Department said its election monitors were “public servants doing a job the Department has done for decades: making sure that every eligible American can cast a ballot free from intimidation and discrimination.”
 A spokeswoman said Justice Department officials had spoken to the New Mexico secretary of state, and the issue had been “resolved.” She also said the monitors in Michigan had asked the same standard questions that had been asked in past elections. Monitors are generally allowed to talk to voters after they have left a polling location.
 The United States has sent monitors out on Election Day since the passage of the 1965 Voting Rights Act in order to ensure public access to the polls, including for people with disabilities. The monitors are also meant to be on the lookout for indications of voter intimidation or suppression based on race, color, national origin or religion. The department’s civil rights division administers the initiative.
 Justice Department lawyers said at a court hearing on Monday that nearly 1,000 people would serve as monitors this year, up from a maximum of about 600 sent out in prior elections. The monitors are department employees but are not supposed to carry guns, display badges or wear law enforcement insignia.
 Often, they stand a set distance away from a polling place in civilian clothes, asking voters about their experience and observations. With more than 100,000 polling places nationwide, the vast majority of voters are unlikely to see, let alone interact with, a federal monitor.
 Even in Republican-led states, the presence of monitors has sometimes drawn scrutiny. During an August primary, Gov. Mark Gordon, Republican of Wyoming, complained publicly after he said the presence of federal monitors had been “aggressive, unexpected, disruptive.”
 This year, the Justice Department sent monitors to several Democratic-leaning areas that it had not visited in 2022 or 2024, including Boston, Chicago, Memphis and Seattle, according to Justice Department news releases. Because the program is meant to protect minority voting rights, it is not unusual for monitors to be stationed in areas with high concentrations of minority voters.
 In the cafeteria of Henry Ford High School in Detroit, Justice Department monitors walked around for about 15 minutes making notes on clipboards on Tuesday morning, poll workers and other observers who saw them later told a New York Times reporter.
 The monitors asked what seemed to be standard questions about accessibility for disabled voters and whether the machines were operating normally, the workers said.
 “They were satisfied with what they saw and how things were running,” said Loretta Wade, who oversaw special terminals for disabled voters.
 Reporting was contributed by Eileen Sullivan , Reis Thebault , Zolan Kanno-Youngs and Neil Vigdor

 Election data reporter We’re watching a few key areas as polls close in Maine and Michigan. 
 Image In 2020, Senator Susan Collins fared well in Bangor, Maine, where she resides, narrowly winning the Democratic-leaning city even as President Trump lost it by 21 points. Credit... Lexi Parra/The New York Times The Senate contests in Maine and Michigan will be rare tests of progressive Democrats’ appeal in battleground states. There are a few key areas we are focusing on as polls at 8 p.m.
 Both of the states have large numbers of Democratic voters, but President Trump won Michigan in 2024 and Senator Susan Collins won Maine in 2020. This year’s Democratic candidates — Troy Jackson in Maine and Dr. Abdul El-Sayed in Michigan — will try to win back coalitions that have recently swung away from the party.
 It’s a marathon in Michigan, not a sprint.
 Grand Rapids
 Ann Arbor
 Detroit
 Oakland County
 Wayne County
 Saginaw County
 Areas to watch in the Michigan Senate race
 Malika Khurana/The New York Times
 Michigan counts its votes relatively slowly. In 2024, when this year’s Republican nominee, Mike Rogers, came within 20,000 votes of victory, only around half of the state’s ballots had been counted by midnight Eastern. If the margin is particularly close, there’s a decent chance we will be waiting on Wayne County , the most populous county in the state and one that is teeming with Democrats. It is also usually among the last to finish reporting its votes: In the August primary, Wayne had not reported 90 percent of its results until around 3 a.m. Eastern.
 Dr. El-Sayed expects to draw a lot of support in Wayne — Kamala Harris won the county by around 250,000 votes in 2024 — but shifts inside the county could be critical to his overall success. In particular, we will be watching Dearborn, Dearborn Heights, and Hamtramck, a group of Wayne cities with large Arab and Muslim populations that made large shifts toward Mr. Trump in 2024. Those shifts were motivated at least in part by President Biden’s handling of the war in Gaza, which should not apply to Dr. El-Sayed, a vocal critic of the United States’ policies toward Israel.
 Conversely, Mr. Rogers will hope to cut into Democratic margins in the suburban Oakland County , which he lost by 12 percentage points in the 2024 Senate race. Dr. El-Sayed could be vulnerable there after losing Oakland in the Democratic primary to Representative Haley Stevens, who represents most of the county in Congress, and endorsed Mr. Rogers’ Senate bid following a highly public feud with Dr. El-Sayed. Both men have made appeals to Michigan’s Jewish voters, a large share of whom reside in Oakland.
 Things could also be interesting in Saginaw County , a key swing region that Mr. Rogers lost by nine votes in 2024 even as Mr. Trump narrowly carried the county (and the state) on the same ballot. A victory for Dr. El-Sayed in Saginaw would be an encouraging sign for his prospects statewide.
 Collins needs as many split-ticket voters as she can get.
 Areas to watch in the Maine Senate race
 Portland
 Aroostook County
 Bangor
 Cumberland
 Scarborough
 Malika Khurana/The New York Times
 At first glance, Maine is much friendlier for Democrats than other states where Republican incumbents are being challenged: Mr. Trump lost the state in all three of his presidential campaigns. But the other Democratic candidates for Senate aren’t facing Ms. Collins, who defied the polls and won re-election by more than eight percentage points in 2020, even as Mr. Trump lost Maine by nine.
 Maine reports its election results by municipality, and there are nearly 500 of them in the state. In 2020, Ms. Collins proved particularly strong in high-income municipalities where a majority of voters are college-educated, like Cumberland (where she ran ahead of Mr. Trump by 27 percentage points in 2020) and Scarborough (where she ran ahead by 23). She also fared well in Bangor , where she resides, narrowly winning the Democratic-leaning city even as Mr. Trump lost it by 21 points.
 Far to the north, Ms. Collins also fared quite well in Aroostook County in 2020, home to Caribou , where she was born and raised. Her strength there will be tested: Mr. Jackson, a fellow Aroostook native, represented much of the area in the state legislature for decades.
 In the event neither candidate reaches 50 percent of the vote, the contest will be decided via ranked-choice tabulation, a process which took ten days in both 2024 and the June primary.

 Election data reporter We’re watching several areas in Texas as polls close there. 
 Image Credit... Elena Shao/The New York Times In Texas, the Senate race between James Talarico, a Democratic state legislator, and Ken Paxton, the Republican attorney general, will play out across 254 counties that include a wide mix of densely packed urban centers and spread-out rural areas.
 There are a few areas we will be focusing on as the results map starts to fill after polls close at 8 p.m. Eastern in most of the state. Across the state, we will be looking at Hispanic voters , who may be shifting back to the left after fueling President Trump’s victory in 2024. Texas, with numerous majority-Hispanic counties, and large Hispanic populations in its urban centers as well, has some of the easiest trends to spot in that crucial demographic. We will also be watching swing voters in the suburbs, who Mr. Talarico has targeted to help combat Mr. Paxton’s strength in rural areas.
 Houston metro area
 Harris County , home to Houston, is the state’s largest by population. In 2008, Barack Obama became the first Democratic presidential candidate to win Harris since 1964. It narrowly flipped back to Republicans in 2012 but has since voted Democratic. Mr. Talarico is likely to carry the county, but the margin may vary: Joseph R. Biden Jr. won it by more than 13 percentage points in 2020, but Kamala Harris won it by less than six percentage points in 2024, as Black and Hispanic areas in Houston swung to the right .
 Houston suburbs of note include the Democratic-leaning Fort Bend County , where Black and Hispanic voters saw similar rightward shifts, and Montgomery County , a rapidly growing Republican stronghold where President Trump won by about 46 percentage points in 2024.
 Dallas-Fort Worth
 Anchored by Fort Worth, Tarrant County has historically been one of Texas’ most populous conservative counties, but it has swung back and forth in recent statewide elections.
 In 2018, Beto O’Rourke won Tarrant by less than a percentage point in his unsuccessful bid for Senate — the first time a Democrat had won the county in a statewide race in decades. Mr. Biden narrowly carried it in 2020 before flipping back to Mr. Trump in 2024. This year, the county has been a focus for both candidates : Mr. Talarico is aiming to replicate — or improve upon — Mr. O’Rourke’s success, while Mr. Paxton is seeking to keep his party’s hold on a crucial source of votes.
 Collin and Denton , the northern Dallas suburbs, are redder than Tarrant, but they also trended somewhat leftward in recent years before moving back toward Mr. Trump in 2024.
 Austin metro area
 Mr. Talarico’s home base is the area around Austin. He represents parts of Travis County in the state legislature and grew up in neighboring Williamson. The Austin suburbs of Williamson and Hays could prove especially insightful. Hays has had a higher share of Democratic voters in the past, but Williamson will cast more than twice as many votes. Mr. Trump won Williamson by two percentage points in 2024, but if it moves back to the Democratic column, that would be a boon to Mr. Talarico’s chances.
 Bexar and El Paso counties
 Hispanic voters have been a crucial swing group in recent years, and they are a key reason the Texas Senate race is in play. In 2024, they were nearly evenly split in Texas between Ms. Harris and Mr. Trump, according to Times Voter Trends , but there are signs they are moving back toward Democrats.
 Bexar , which includes San Antonio, is the state’s most populous majority-Hispanic county. Results there could offer indications of how that demographic is leaning in urban areas. El Paso has similar dynamics, though it will begin reporting its results an hour later because it is on Mountain time.
 South Texas and the border
 The rural counties in South Texas, particularly in the Rio Grande Valley, will also help illuminate understanding of the shifts among Hispanic voters. The counties there are heavily Hispanic and have been shifting rightward since 2016. In 2024, Mr. Trump won them outright, flipping them from blue to red. Cameron and Hidalgo are the most populous, but smaller counties in the area with similar demographic profiles like Starr, or others close to the border like Jim Hogg or Kenedy, could show early signs of the region’s voting patterns.
 Rural Texas
 More than 100 small, reliably red counties across rural Texas are expected to be sources of strength for Mr. Paxton. They tend to report results hours after polls close and are likely to include nearly all of their votes in their first report. By contrast, larger counties typically report early votes first, with Election Day votes coming in a few hours later.
 The early votes from large counties could be favorable to Mr. Talarico, but the margin is expected to narrow as the vast bloc of rural counties report their votes.

 Here’s why some states take longer to count and report their results. 
 Image Workers receiving mail-in ballots in a sorting area in Santa Ana, Calif. The state’s emphasis on voting by mail often leads to a slower vote count, election experts said. Credit... Apu Gomes/Getty Images It’s Election Day, an exercise in democracy that seemingly never fails to leave Americans hanging on every last ballot to be counted.
 Gather your patience, and some caffeine, as experts say it may take several days, if not longer, for complete results to emerge, introducing an element of uncertainty to races that could decide control the Senate, House and governorships.
 The waiting game is expected to raise a recurring question in U.S. elections: Why are some states much slower to report results than others?
 “Slow is in the eye of the beholder,” said David Scott, vice president of elections for The Associated Press. (Many news media outlets, including The New York Times , rely on the news organization’s race calls.)
 What usually causes counting delays?
 Voting by mail, which gained in popularity during the coronavirus pandemic, has become increasingly common in several states, particularly in the West . But, experts said, that convenience does not always lend itself to the speed of processing and counting ballots.
 Six states, including Wisconsin and Pennsylvania, do not allow election officials to begin processing those ballots until Election Day, according to the National Conference of State Legislatures .
 Machines that can open envelopes can help speed the process, but many places have not upgraded their technology, often because of the expense, said Tammy Patrick, chief programs officer at the National Association of Election Officials.
 As a result, election workers, one Republican and one Democrat, must open the envelopes by hand.
 “There’s a saying that we often use in elections,” Ms. Patrick said. “We want our elections to be cheap, fast and accurate, but we only get to pick two things.”
 While many states require absentee ballots to be returned by Election Day, some allow for them to be received up to 10 or 15 days later, as long as they are postmarked by Election Day.
 Who’s in for a long night?
 California, the nation’s most populous state, is an obvious contender because of its emphasis on voting by mail, experts said.
 During the presidential election in 2024, when nearly 81 percent of residents cast ballots by mail, about 60 percent of the state’s vote was counted by election night, according to The Associated Press.
 “It’s part of what they have chosen to value, which is maximum participation,” Mr. Scott said.
 It’s not just states that have developed a reputation of lumbering through an election. So have some cities critical to Democrats, two of which could tip races for the control of the Senate.
 In Texas, Harris County — its seat is Houston, and it is the most populous in the state — is often a straggler in reporting its election results. That’s something that those who track results said to keep in mind in the Senate race between James Talarico, the Democratic nominee, and Ken Paxton, the Republican nominee and the state attorney general, whom polls have shown to be in a tight contest.
 In Michigan, Wayne County, which includes Detroit, has experienced similar counting delays in past elections that experts said could significantly loom over the Senate race between Mike Rogers, a Republican former representative, and Dr. Abdul El-Sayed, the Democratic nominee.
 Ms. Patrick, of the National Association of Election Officials, said many people lose sight of the fact that not a single state in the nation reports official results on election night.
 “The real tension here is when the races are close and whether or not the media are comfortable projecting to winners,” she said.
 What about ranked-choice voting?
 Two states with pivotal Senate races, Maine and Alaska, use ranked-choice voting, in which voters select a set number of candidates in order of preference.
 If no candidate captures 50 percent of the vote in the first round of counting, additional rounds follow, which experts said could result in delays of several days in those states.
 Like other New England states, Maine has a highly decentralized election system in which votes are reported at the municipal level, which analysts said could create delays.
 And Alaska, because of its large size and more extensive grace period for returning absentee ballots, could also take longer to settle.
 Counting of absentee ballots begins on election night at five regional elections offices in Alaska, which does not require voters to have a reason for choosing to vote by mail. The state accepts absentee ballots that are postmarked by Election Day until 10 days after an election if mailed from within the United States and up to 15 days after if mailed from overseas.
 Who’s in for an early night?
 Election experts pointed to Florida as one of the fastest states to report election results.
 It does not allow same-day voter registration and requires absentee ballots to be received by 7 p.m. local time on Election Day.
 The emphasis on speed and tightening of voting rules came after Florida was widely criticized during the 2000 election, when the outcome of the presidential race hinged on ballot problems and a protracted recount in the state.
 “States make choices,” Mr. Scott said.
